analysis.one_liner: Repeals the federal estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes.
analysis.headline: The estate tax repeal bill drew five Republican cosponsors, received no committee action after its referral to Ways and Means, and died when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would wipe out the federal estate tax, the gift tax, and the tax on generation-skipping transfers — the taxes owed when very large amounts of wealth are passed to heirs or given away [S2] [S3]. The repeal would apply to deaths and transfers after the bill's enactment [S3]. It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced and never moved from there [S1] [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: The heirs of very large estates. The federal estate tax applies only to estates above a multi-million-dollar exemption, so repeal channels billions of dollars to a few thousand of the wealthiest families each year; the gift and generation-skipping taxes they would otherwise owe on lifetime transfers also disappear [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_pays: The federal treasury, and ultimately taxpayers and recipients of federal services, who would either face the lost revenue as more borrowing or make it up through other taxes or cuts; the wealth passed to heirs of large estates would instead go untaxed [S2] [S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill would eliminate a tax that by design falls only on very large transfers of wealth, converting billions in annual revenue into untaxed inheritance for the wealthiest families while leaving the rest of the tax code unchanged to absorb the loss [S2] [S3].
Because the repeal takes effect immediately upon enactment rather than phasing in, the entire revenue loss would hit the budget in the first full year [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains go almost entirely to heirs of the largest estates, while the lost revenue must be recovered from everyone else through borrowing, other taxes, or service cuts. For households far below the estate-tax threshold, the bill offers nothing and costs something.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it expired without a floor vote when the 106th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Joseph Pitts (R-PA) introduced the bill on January 6, 1999, to repeal the estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes [S1] [S3].
The House referred it to the Committee on Ways and Means that same day, and the action history shows no hearing, markup, or vote ever followed [S1] [S5].
Five Republicans cosponsored the bill and no Democrat did [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The general treasury and the taxpayers who fund it, since estate and gift tax revenue continued to be collected; no one gained the repeal's benefits because it never advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The federal treasury and general taxpayers

for.name: Rep. Joseph Pitts
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the estate, gift, and generation-skipping taxes and referred it to Ways and Means.

against.name: Rep. Bill Archer
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after its referral; no hearing or markup was ever scheduled and it never reached the House floor.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all five cosponsors were Republicans, with no Democrats joining, and the bill drew no action in a committee chaired by a Republican.

industries.note: Repeal would have eliminated the estate, gift, and generation-skipping taxes that fall only on very large transfers of wealth, letting billions a year pass to heirs untaxed while the general fund absorbs the lost revenue [S2] [S3]. The bill died, so the tax remained in place.
